Split illustration contrasting traditional and modern biotechnology. Left half (warm earthy colours): a Nigerian kitchen scene with a calabash of frothing palm wine, a jute sack of grated cassava being pressed under a heavy stone for garri, a clay pot of fermenting ogi, and leaf-wrapped bundles of iru. Right half (cool blue and steel colours): a stainless steel fermenter tank with pipes and a control panel, a scientist in a lab coat with a pipette, a petri dish of bacterial colonies, a DNA double helix and test tubes holding small plantlets in jelly.

Step-by-step diagram of plant tissue culture in six panels from left to right. 1: a healthy plantain (or cassava) parent plant with a highlighted shoot tip. 2: a gloved hand with a scalpel cutting a tiny explant from the shoot tip, beside a beaker of sterilising solution. 3: a glass jar containing clear jelly medium with the explant on its surface. 4: a jar with a lump of pale callus tissue. 5: a jar with several small green shoots and white roots. 6: young plantlets in small pots in a greenhouse, then planted in a field row.

A legume plant (soybean or cowpea) pulled from the soil showing its roots covered with small round pink-brown root nodules. An enlarged inset of a cut nodule shows many tiny rod-shaped Rhizobium bacteria inside the root cells, with arrows showing N2 from the air in the soil entering and ammonium compounds passing to the plant. Beside it, a packet of Rhizobium inoculant powder being mixed with seeds.

A culture plate (petri dish) seen from above, covered with many small cream-coloured bacterial colonies, with a fuzzy blue-green mould colony near one edge surrounded by a clear ring with no bacteria. Beside it, a simple portrait-free sketch of the mould under magnification showing branching hyphae and brush-like spore-bearing structures.

Labelled cross-section of an industrial fermenter: a tall stainless steel cylinder with a motor-driven stirrer shaft and paddles inside, a water jacket around the outside with cold water in at the bottom and warm water out at the top, a sterile air inlet with a sparger (bubble ring) at the bottom, a nutrient inlet at the top, an exhaust gas outlet at the top, temperature and pH probes on the side, and a harvest outlet tap at the bottom. Inside, a cloudy culture with tiny fungal threads.

Flow diagram of garri production in six steps from left to right: 1 fresh cassava roots being peeled with a knife; 2 white peeled roots being washed and grated into a pulp in a bowl; 3 a jute sack of wet pulp squeezed under heavy stones on wooden planks with water dripping out; 4 a close-up circle inset of the pulp with tiny rod-shaped bacteria and oval yeast cells; 5 a woman sieving the mash through a raffia sieve; 6 the mash being roasted in a wide iron pan over a firewood fire, and a bowl of finished yellow and white garri.
